n: Two more years passed with Joseph forgotten in prison. Then Pharaoh dreamed he was standing by the Nile, the river that was Egypt’s lifeline.

f.g: the Nile, source of all Egypt’s farming and wealth

n: Seven healthy, well-fed cows came up out of the Nile to graze in the reeds by the river.

f.g: Hebrew ’aḥu, an Egyptian word for the reed grass along the Nile

n: Then seven ugly, scrawny cows came up and stood beside them on the riverbank.
Shockingly, the thin cows ate the fat cows—something unnatural and alarming. Pharaoh woke up.
In a second dream, seven plump heads of grain grew on a single stalk.

f.g: In the KJV “corn” means grain in general (wheat, barley), not maize.

n: Then seven thin heads, scorched by the hot desert east wind, sprouted after them.

f.g: scorched by the hot, dry wind from the desert (the sirocco)

n: The thin heads swallowed the full ones. Pharaoh woke and realized it was a dream—but it felt deeply significant.
Pharaoh was disturbed and summoned Egypt’s magicians and wise men, the experts in dream interpretation, but none could explain it.

f.g: Hebrew ḥarṭummim — Egyptian priest-scholars skilled in sacred writings

n: At last the cupbearer remembered Joseph and admitted his failure to mention him.

f.g: my offenses (both his old offense and his forgetfulness)

n: The cupbearer recalls being jailed with the baker in Potiphar’s house.
He recounts that both of them had meaningful dreams the same night.
He describes Joseph modestly as a young Hebrew slave—but one who interpreted their dreams accurately.
The proof: everything happened exactly as Joseph said. One was restored, one was executed.
Pharaoh summoned Joseph immediately. Joseph shaved and changed clothes to appear properly before Pharaoh, since Egyptians were clean-shaven.
Pharaoh tells Joseph he has heard Joseph can interpret dreams.
Joseph humbly corrects him: “It is not in me”—God will give the answer. He gives God the credit before the most powerful man on earth.
Pharaoh retells his dream, beginning by the Nile.
He describes the seven healthy cows grazing in the reeds.
Pharaoh adds his own emotion: he had never seen such ugly cows in all Egypt.
The thin cows devoured the fat ones.
Pharaoh adds a detail: after eating, the lean cows looked as thin as ever. The coming famine would be so severe it would wipe out any memory of plenty.
Pharaoh describes the second dream of the seven good heads of grain.
He describes the withered, scorched heads that followed.
The thin heads swallowed the good ones, and none of the magicians could explain it.
Joseph explains: the two dreams carry one message. God is revealing to Pharaoh what He is about to do.

f.w: God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do

n: The seven good cows and seven good heads both stand for seven years of abundance.
The seven thin cows and scorched heads stand for seven years of famine.
Joseph repeats that God is showing Pharaoh the future—so Pharaoh can prepare.
First will come seven years of great abundance across Egypt.
Then seven years of famine so severe that people will forget the good years ever happened.
The famine will be so harsh that the abundance will leave no trace.
Getting the dream twice meant it was certain and coming soon. In scripture, repetition often confirms a divine message.
Joseph moves from interpretation to counsel: appoint a wise, discerning man to manage Egypt.
His plan: appoint officials and store a fifth of the harvest during the good years—a careful, practical strategy of preparation.

f.g: a 20 percent tax on the harvest

n: Grain should be collected and stored in cities under Pharaoh’s authority.
The stored food would keep the country alive through the famine. Latter-day Saints often see in this a pattern for self-reliance and food storage.
Pharaoh and his officials liked the plan.
Pharaoh recognizes that Joseph has the Spirit of God—remarkable words from a pagan king.

f.w: a man in whom the Spirit of God is

n: Pharaoh concludes that no one is wiser than the man God has taught.
Pharaoh makes Joseph his second-in-command over the palace and kingdom. Only the throne would remain Pharaoh’s.

f.w: according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled

n: In a single day Joseph went from prisoner to governor of Egypt—God’s timing had arrived.
Pharaoh gave Joseph symbols of authority: his signet ring (for sealing official documents), royal linen clothing, and a gold chain. Once stripped of his robes, Joseph is now clothed with honor.

f.g: robes of fine linen, worn by Egyptian nobility

n: Joseph rode in the second chariot, and heralds shouted for people to bow—fulfilling his boyhood dreams in an unexpected way.

f.g: Hebrew ’abrek, possibly an Egyptian word meaning “Attention!” or “Make way!”

n: Pharaoh confirms Joseph’s total authority: nothing in Egypt would happen without his permission.
Pharaoh gave Joseph an Egyptian name and a noble wife, the daughter of a priest of On (Heliopolis), a major center of sun worship.

f.g: Egyptian name; meaning debated, perhaps “God speaks and he lives” or “revealer of secrets.”

n: Joseph was thirty—thirteen years after being sold at seventeen. Like Christ beginning His ministry at about thirty, Joseph now begins his great work of saving lives.
The harvests during the good years were enormous, just as foretold.
Joseph collected the surplus and stored each region’s grain in its nearby city.
So much grain was stored that they stopped counting—“like the sand of the sea,” the same image used for Abraham’s countless descendants.

f.w: as the sand of the sea

n: Before the famine came, Joseph and Asenath had two sons.
Joseph named his firstborn Manasseh (“causing to forget”) because God had healed the pain of his hardships and separation from home.
His second son was named Ephraim (“doubly fruitful”), because God made him prosper in a land of suffering. Ephraim would later receive the birthright blessing.
The seven abundant years came to an end, as foretold.
Famine struck every land around, but Egypt had bread because of Joseph’s inspired preparation.
When the Egyptians cried for food, Pharaoh sent them to Joseph: “Whatever he says to you, do it.” Mary would later say almost the same words about Jesus at Cana.

f.w: what he saith to you, do

n: As the famine spread, Joseph opened the storehouses and sold grain to the people.
People from every country came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph—setting the stage for his brothers’ arrival. Joseph became a savior to the world of his day.
